profiles.name: Prometheus
profiles.summary: Open-source Lua 5.1 / basic Luau obfuscator written in Lua (levno-710).

versions.label: as measured (no version split)

methods.note: structure matched against the tool's own source and its real output

samples.notes: Fixtures were made by running the real tool on programs written for this project.

runtime.runtimes: PUC Lua 5.1 / LuaJIT / Lua 5.4 via lupa

reproduction.note: fixtures re-measured on a fresh machine; verdict changes: 0

limitations: Vmify (the flattened register VM) is unflattened: the dispatcher is walked, every block is turned back into statements and the control flow is rebuilt (also for the two Vmify layers of the Strong preset). The output behaves like the obfuscated script on real Lua 5.1; the original variable and function names are not in the output and cannot be recovered.

The anti-tamper check that Medium and Strong compile into the VM is removed by taint analysis when it is separable from the program; if a script mixes the two it is left alone and the step reports why.
String decoders (EncryptStrings, ConstantArray) are evaluated only when sandboxed evaluation is switched on.
Recovery of the Strong preset takes several seconds in the browser (the two layers are rebuilt one after the other).

verification.basis: fixtures made by the real tool, behaviour decided on reference runtimes

unversioned.why: 87 of 91 real-tool fixtures reconstructed with identical behaviour on a reference runtime (lower bound 89%).

profiles.name: MoonVeil
profiles.summary: Commercial obfuscator (moonveil.cc) with selectable virtualisation, function encryption and control-flow flattening (macros MV_VM, MV_ENC_FUNC, MV_CFF, MV_OMIT). One real output was read (banner "generated using MoonVeil 2.0.25"): functions lifted into a table, flattened bootstrap code, Z85 + XOR strings, bit32 expressions for numbers, and VM-compiled functions stored as one compressed Z85 text (read back from that data by the VM reader when the interpreter has the shape of the script that was studied).

versions.label: as measured (no version split)

methods.note: banner comment

samples.notes: No real output of this tool was available.

limitations: Read back statically from the one script: the strings (Z85 text plus an XOR cipher), the numbers (bit32 expressions) and the table of cells, which makes the program’s plain Lua readable.

The function MoonVeil compiled to its own VM is read back too, without running anything. How its data is laid out (field ids, opcode table, instruction layouts), which cell of the interpreter is which builtin and what its helper methods do are all taken from the script’s own interpreter code, so they are not fixed in this tool. The data is decoded, the encrypted part of it is opened by searching for the one small number its key depends on, and every instruction is partially evaluated against the interpreter’s own handlers and structured back into Lua.

A build whose interpreter has a different shape is not guessed at: the step says which part did not fit and the general passes take over. Only version 2.0.25 and one script were looked at, so other builds and settings (MV_CFF, MV_ENC_FUNC) are unconfirmed.

Not compared with a run of the original: the report says so and keeps the confidence at medium. A generic for loop of a shape the reader does not know stays as a call to forgprep (the VM’s own step; none is left in the script that was studied), and register capture follows the VM’s model rather than Lua’s scoping, so a few locals are shared where the source had separate ones.

verification.basis: recovery measured on examples that are not real tool output

unversioned.why: The output can be recognised. No reconstruction has been verified against real or authorised samples.

profiles.name: IronBrew 2
profiles.summary: Open-source (MIT) Lua 5.1 obfuscator in C# that compiles a script with luac and re-emits it as a custom register VM plus a compressed, XOR-masked program string.

versions.label: as measured (no version split)

methods.note: structure matched against the tool's own source and its real output

samples.notes: Fixtures were made by running the real tool on programs written for this project.

runtime.runtimes: PUC Lua 5.1 / LuaJIT / Lua 5.4 via lupa

reproduction.note: fixtures re-measured on a fresh machine; verdict changes: 0

limitations: Recovery reads the embedded chunk instead of running the VM: handlers are identified by shape, operand transforms are solved symbolically, the Lua 5.1 chunk is rebuilt and decompiled. A handler that matches no template stops the recovery with an error instead of guessing.
Local variable names, comments and the original function layout are not in the bytecode, so they are not recoverable (names are regenerated; some local functions come back as expressions).

The "strings" option decrypts every literal with a routine written out in place. Recovery finds those stretches (only constants, only pure standard functions, no closures) and replaces each by the text it computes, using the sandbox interpreter on that stretch alone; it needs no consent because nothing but the stretch is run. Other register-reuse noise remains, so the result is partial.

The "flow" option of the real tool produced output that does not run correctly on its own for five of eight samples (see the "tool broken" column); recovery there is judged against the original program, not against the broken output.
Only IronBrew 2 as built from the public MIT source is covered. Forks that change the VM template or the serialiser need their own templates.

verification.basis: fixtures made by the real tool, behaviour decided on reference runtimes

unversioned.why: 64 of 64 real-tool fixtures reconstructed with identical behaviour on a reference runtime (lower bound 94%).

limitations: Literal, folded and string.char payloads are unwrapped without running anything. A payload computed by a decoder (hex, base64, XOR, URL escapes, ...) is read only when sandboxed evaluation is on, and only when the script is nothing but that loader: the other statements may use standard libraries and local variables, nothing else.
A script that does anything else around the loader (touches the game, writes globals, prints) is never replaced wholesale; Dump still shows the text it loads.
Payloads that read `...`, return values, or need the network (`HttpGet`) are left alone. Compiled Lua 5.1 and 5.4 payloads are decompiled.

These are generic packers I wrote from the encodings other tools document. Whether a real obfuscator that uses the same encodings is handled depends on its decoder staying within the standard libraries; none of them was run.

verification.basis: recovery measured on examples that are not real tool output

profiles.name: Colisseum
profiles.summary: Open-source (AGPL-3.0) Lua / Luau obfuscator written in Lua (de-TourLLC). Presets easy, medium, hard and full are source-level; total and fortress compile the program for a VM.

versions.label: as measured (no version split)

methods.note: structure matched against the tool's own source and its real output

characteristics.text: tamper guard (debug hook, executor globals, replaced standard functions, line-number check)

samples.notes: Fixtures were made by running the real tool on programs written for this project.

runtime.runtimes: PUC Lua 5.1 / LuaJIT / Lua 5.4 via lupa

reproduction.note: fixtures re-measured on a fresh machine; verdict changes: 0

limitations: easy, medium, hard and full are source-level: the tamper guard is recognised by its strings and removed without being run, the string decryptor is evaluated in the sandbox, and the junk branches are dropped. The output prints what the original program prints; names are guesses from use.

The decryptor multiplies past 2^53 and was written for Lua 5.4 integers (it gives noise on Lua 5.1, LuaJIT and Luau doubles). The sandbox therefore evaluates it both ways and keeps the reading that is text; if neither is, the strings are left encoded and the report says so. Without the sandbox the strings stay encoded.

total (native VM) and fortress (register VM with an encrypted bytecode blob) are detected from the VM entry call and flagged as not recovered: the program exists only as data for an interpreter. Recovery is not attempted.

The behavioural trace is stopped by the tamper guard of every preset except easy, because the trace’s stand-in environment defines executor functions and the guard counts them (error 0x6B0C). Remove the guard first (medium, hard, full: Deobfuscate, then Trace the result). In the plain sandbox total runs to the end and fortress stops at 0x3E44 (the guard sees the sandbox’s debug library is not native).
The total and fortress fixtures only run without an instruction-count hook, on LuaJIT: their anti-tamper treats a hook as an attack, so they were verified with tests/corpus/tools/run_lua_nohook.py.

verification.basis: fixtures made by the real tool, behaviour decided on reference runtimes

unversioned.why: 32 of 48 reconstructed with identical behaviour (lower bound 53%).

profiles.name: Simple-Lua-Obfuscator
profiles.summary: Small obfuscator (CloudHub111, no licence file): the script is written as codes, base64-encoded, cut into five-character pieces and loaded at run time.

reproduction.note: fixtures re-measured on a fresh machine; verdict changes: 0

limitations: The program is written as decimal escapes, base64-encoded, cut into five-character pieces and loaded at run time. With the sandbox on, the loader is run alone to read the text it hands to load, and that text replaces the script. Without the sandbox the layer is only detected.

This is a loader-style packer: anything the loader does besides decoding (touching other globals, printing) stops the replacement. Variable names of the original are kept because the payload is the original source.

profiles.name: AzureVM
profiles.summary: Open-source (MIT) Lua 5.1 VM obfuscator by LionHub-Pino, built on Prometheus. Reads Lua 5.1 bytecode and emits an interpreter with an encoded payload: seeded opcode map, rolling instruction encoding, per-prototype field layouts. Preset names with "Luraph" in them are its own labels (its README says it is not Luraph); its payload is tagged "LPH" like Luraph’s.

versions.label: as measured (no version split)

methods.note: structure matched against the tool's own source and its real output

samples.notes: Fixtures were made by running the real tool on programs written for this project.

runtime.runtimes: PUC Lua 5.1 / LuaJIT / Lua 5.4 via lupa

reproduction.note: fixtures re-measured on a fresh machine; verdict changes: 0

limitations: The program is compiled to Lua 5.1 bytecode, its instructions are encoded with a seeded opcode map and a rolling cipher, and a generated interpreter runs it. The VM is detected and flagged as not recovered; no lifter for this format was written.
The Balanced preset is not a VM: its Prometheus-style transforms are partly reverted by the existing passes.

Presets named after Luraph are the tool’s own labels; its README says it is not Luraph. The payload tag LPH is the same three letters Luraph uses, which is a naming overlap, not evidence of shared code.
Fixtures were generated here by running the tool inside the isolated harness; its outputs are committed because the licence is MIT.

verification.basis: fixtures made by the real tool, behaviour decided on reference runtimes

unversioned.why: 47 of 48 real-tool fixtures reconstructed with identical behaviour on a reference runtime (lower bound 89%).

profiles.name: Simple Open source Lua Obfuscator (page)
profiles.summary: A single HTML page (iamsopotatoe, MIT) that strips comments, renames locals with regular expressions, encodes strings for a _D decoder, writes numbers as sums, and adds junk statements and always-true wrappers. Its author says it gives no meaningful protection and may break code.

versions.label: as measured (no version split)

methods.note: structure matched against the tool's own source and its real output

characteristics.text: string codes with a key decoder

samples.notes: Fixtures were made by running the real tool on programs written for this project.

runtime.runtimes: PUC Lua 5.1 / LuaJIT / Lua 5.4 via lupa

reproduction.note: fixtures re-measured on a fresh machine; verdict changes: 0

limitations: The page renames locals by regular expression (so it can break code that its author did not test) and writes strings as number lists for the _D decoder. The decoder is a subtraction with wrap-around, recognised only in the exact form the page writes it and computed on the literal lists, so no sandbox is needed.
Three of the eight outputs of the page itself do not behave like their originals (its regular-expression renaming breaks some programs), so behaviour is only compared for the other five.
The author says in the page itself that it gives no meaningful protection. The numbers here measure how much of the original is recovered, not how strong the tool is.

verification.basis: fixtures made by the real tool, behaviour decided on reference runtimes

unversioned.why: 5 of 8 reconstructed with identical behaviour (lower bound 31%).

limitations: The rename and string/flow modes are reverted statically. The VM modes (vm, vm-max) hide the program behind a stack or register VM and are detected and flagged as not recovered.

The repository’s README warns of rebrands and sellers using the name. The header seen in output is the hosted service’s, so a script with it may come from the service rather than from the open-source build; this is not a finding about who made a script.
vm-max (LZSS plus a cipher layer) could not be run on the reference interpreters here, so its behaviour was not compared.
